title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is an abuse-of-access failure rather than a technical one. A license plate reader system built for law enforcement lookups was used by the official who controlled it to check the whereabouts of a private individual, repeatedly, over a period of months. The tool worked as designed. The failure was that nothing between the chief and the query data asked why he was asking.

The misuse sat at the point of individual queries, which is where the system's own records would have shown it. Catching it would have required someone reviewing who ran lookups and on what grounds, and the reporting does not describe any such check operating during the period in question. The conduct surfaced through a certification process after the chief had already resigned, not through oversight of the system.

The account rests on a single outlet's report of a Kansas certification order, and the headline and the order as summarized give different counts of the lookups, 164 and 228, which the available facts do not reconcile. The order is an administrative finding, not a criminal verdict, and no court ruling is described.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: According to a Kansas certification order, Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license plate readers 228 times from June to October 2023 to check the whereabouts of his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend. The order said he also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted jealousy influenced his conduct. Nygaard resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
